description: Commercial banks facilitate the flow of money in the economy by accepting deposits and providing loans. When borrowers fail to repay their loans, these advances turn into Non-Performing Assets (NPAs), which negatively impact the stability and profitability of the banking system.

sections.title: Introduction and History of Commercial Banks
sections.description: The basic definition of commercial banks, their classifications, and the history of bank nationalization in India.

key_concepts.explanation: Financial institutions that accept deposits from the general public and provide loans or advances with the primary objective of earning a profit.
Banks that are listed in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934, and meet specific criteria regarding paid-up capital and reserves.
The ability of commercial banks to expand the money supply in the economy by issuing multiple loans based on initial primary deposits, heavily influenced by the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR).

historical_events.significance: 14 major private commercial banks with deposits of over Rs. 50 crore were nationalized to expand the banking network and ensure credit flow to priority sectors like agriculture.
Six more private banks with deposits of over Rs. 200 crore were brought under public ownership, bringing a vast majority of the banking sector under government control.

important_facts.fact: The State Bank of India (SBI) is the largest commercial bank and Public Sector Bank (PSB) in India.

sections.title: Non-Performing Assets: Definition and Classification
sections.description: Criteria for identifying NPAs and the classification of bad loans based on their duration of default.

key_concepts.explanation: A loan or advance for which the principal or interest payment remains overdue for a period of more than 90 days.
An NPA that has remained in the non-performing category for a period of 12 months or less.
An asset that has remained in the sub-standard category for a period of more than 12 months.
An asset that has been identified as uncollectible by the bank or internal/external auditors but has not yet been wholly written off from the books of account.

important_facts.fact: For agricultural loans, an advance is declared an NPA if the installment of principal or interest remains unpaid for two crop seasons (for short-duration crops) or one crop season (for long-duration crops).

sections.title: Impacts of NPAs and Banking Norms
sections.description: The macroeconomic impact of bad loans and international banking norms designed to mitigate financial risks.

key_concepts.explanation: A macroeconomic scenario where corporate houses are heavily over-leveraged (in deep debt) and banks have massive accumulations of bad loans, leading to a freeze in fresh investments.
The percentage of funds that a bank must set aside from its profits to cover potential losses arising from its bad loans.
The ratio of a bank's capital to its risk-weighted assets. It acts as a cushion to absorb unforeseen losses and protects depositors.

important_facts.fact: Under the Basel Norms, the RBI has mandated that Indian scheduled commercial banks must maintain a minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) of 9%.

sections.title: NPA Resolution and Recovery Mechanisms
sections.description: Various legal frameworks and institutional measures implemented by the Government and RBI to recover bad loans and stabilize the banking sector.

key_concepts.explanation: The National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd (NARCL) acts as a 'Bad Bank' by purchasing large bad loans from commercial banks at a discount to help clean up their balance sheets.

A regulatory framework by the RBI under which banks with weak financial metrics (like high NPAs or low capital) are put under watch and restricted from distributing dividends or issuing fresh large loans.

key_associations.extra_info: Empowers banks and financial institutions to auction residential or commercial properties of defaulters to recover loans without the intervention of the court.
Provides a unified and time-bound Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) for resolving bankruptcies of companies and individuals.
A 7-pronged strategy launched by the Government of India to resolve issues faced by PSBs, including recapitalization and professionalization of management.
